segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants gave us dhimahi: we hold in mind, a we even when one voice says it. Today the week comes back around, with three small words.

Half the confusion in any group chat is pronouns. He said he'd bring it. Which he? The Gayatri has the same knot in its second line: dhiyo yo nah. Yo means who. So who is the who: the radiance, or the god? Sanskrit settles it the way it settled tat, with an ending. The answer is the god.
screen: `HE SAID HE'D BRING IT. WHICH HE?`

segments.voice: Here's how a reader knows. The radiance, bhargas, is neuter. Yah, who, is masculine. So it can't point back to the radiance. It points to the one with a masculine name: Savitr, the god. And yah becomes yo before the n of nah, the same -as-to-o kind of join that made bhargo. Dhiyo is dhiyas: thoughts, plural, the whole moving stream. Nah is our. So far, then: who, our thoughts. Now the week, end to end. The map: two verbs, one for the people, one for the god. Tat, that, pointing before it names. Savitur, of Savitr, the sun's light or a light behind seeing. Varenyam, worth choosing, with the tongue curled back. Bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god, which nobody holds. Dhimahi, we hold it in mind, even alone. And today: who, our thoughts. One word is left. The sentence has been waiting all week for its last verb.
screen: `YAH IS MASCULINE: IT MEANS THE GOD.` · `DHIYO: THOUGHTS, PLURAL.` · `NAH: OUR.` · `A WEEK OF ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `WHO, OUR THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound that keeps going on its own: a fan, traffic, a fridge, rain. Let it be the only thing you follow. When a thought pulls you off, notice it, one of the many, and come back to the sound.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece, lightly: dhiyo yo nah, who, our thoughts, and the who is the god.

chat.says: Dad says we keep the Gayatri for home, not stages. fine. but who's the 'who' in it?
options: the god: yo is masculine and the radiance is neuter, so who points to Savitr.
the light: yo points to the nearest noun, and bhargo is right there.
the people praying: yo means you, the one saying it.
chat.meaning: Yah, who, is masculine; the radiance, bhargas, is neuter. So the who is the god Savitr, the one asked to stir our thoughts.

Savitr.meaning: a Rig Veda god of the sun, the one who sets things going

notes: Week end (1499–1505): the look-back recaps days 1499–1504 (map, tat, savitur, varenyam, bhargo devasya, dhimahi); games.recall holds those six pieces (word → line).

Grammar stated: dhiyaḥ accusative plural of dhī; yaḥ masculine relative referring to Savitr (not to neuter bhargas); naḥ enclitic 'our/us'; -aḥ becoming o before voiced y and n. Confirm wording for learners.

Priya's arc: her dad, Arjun, says the family keeps the Gayatri for home, not a stage; this reflects one real view (traditions differ on reciting it publicly; howItsDone names both). She will choose a peace chant for the assembly (1506–1507).
